work.author: Severian of Gabala
work.title: In illud: Secundum imaginem et similitudinem

paragraphs.text: The other day my sermon touched in part on what can be contemplated in creation, but the commotion of the crowd knocked it off its proper course. For nothing weakens the force of what is said so much as an unruly crowd, and nothing so feeds the speaker's confidence as steadiness, calm and quiet, which give the speaker freedom and the hearers understanding. So lend your ears to what is said, and spread out your silence like earth to receive the rain of teaching. A farmer who does not cut his furrow deep cannot set the seeds down in the depth of the soil. In the same way, if deep silence does not make room for the preaching, it clouds the speaker's mind and robs the hearers' souls.

So look at this. As Deuteronomy says, when Moses and the priests and the Levites were about to make a proclamation, they cried out in a clear voice before setting out the divine teachings, as Scripture testifies: "Be silent and hear, O Israel." In the same way blessed David, wishing to show that the divine oracles can only be received with a mind at rest, cries out in the forty-fifth psalm: "Be still, and know that I am God." So, lovers of Christ, be still and make room for the teaching by your silence.

Earlier I said that God made heaven and earth without using any matter that already existed. By his own power he brought matter itself out of nothing, and once he had put it forth, he shaped it to perfection by setting it in order.

Second, we worked through the point that God does not build his creation the way people build. He does not first lay foundations and then put on the roof. Since he himself is the craftsman, the foundation and the support of all that comes to be, he made the roof first and then spread the earth out beneath it.

Third, I put before you that he set the air beneath heaven and placed the water beneath the earth. The foundations he laid are not in proportion to the size of what we see. They are made strong and held together by divine power, and they truly bear witness to the working of their Maker.

Fourth, the wonderful Moses set out for us his account, and in his list of created things he did not mention angels or archangels or any of the powers above. His aim was to correct the error about all the things we see. The things that appear to us were being worshiped: sun and moon and stars, rivers and springs, mountains and sea. So this wonderful man, weaving his account of creation in order and sequence, rightly set out only the visible things and passed over the invisible in silence. In the form of his teaching he could then both point to the One who made them and proclaim his works.

Again, I said that God gave this world to human beings as a school, so that through these elements we might learn his all-wise knowledge. For the heavens declare the glory of God, and all creation proclaims the wisdom of its Craftsman. And see what is wonderful here. God did not give the heavens a mouth or a tongue that can speak. If they had been given spoken words, their teaching would certainly have had only one language, and only those who knew that one language would have benefited. Instead, he gave them sight in place of a voice, and the beauty of what is seen in place of a tongue. They are not seen one way by some and another way by others. All people grasp them equally.
Sixth, I said that creation itself also rebukes the ungrateful.

Seventh, I said that a godly soul, gathering the flowers of all creation's beauties, displays the splendor of the whole created order. Such people are even called lights, as Paul says: "among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast the word of life." And they shine like the sun and like the moon forever, as God testifies in a promise to Adam [?], saying: "And his throne shall be like the sun before me, and like the moon established forever."

In the same way the company of the righteous imitates the beauty of all the other things on earth, as it is written: "How fair are your houses, O Jacob, your tents, O Israel! They are like shady valleys, like a garden beside rivers, like cedars beside the waters." The saints also imitate the swiftness of the eagle: "Your youth will be renewed like the eagle's." And they have the strength of lions: "The righteous man is as confident as a lion." Their imitation rises even to the angels. Those on earth imitate the divine dances of the heavenly choirs. Blessed David shows that the saints share the angels' honor when he says: "I will give thanks to you, O Lord, with my whole heart, and before the angels I will sing your praise." Nor do they stop at imitating the angels. They become imitators of our Lord Jesus Christ himself, as Paul says: "Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ."

Consider what honor a human being attains by being made in the image of God, as we have heard the great lawgiver tell of man. With his words, as if in a painting, he showed heaven embroidered with its stars and earth in bloom with flowers. He sketched the mountain peaks shaded by deep forest, and in short all the order and beauty we can see. Only then, last of all, does he bring in man, who was to be honored above everything visible. So man is fashioned last in the work of creation but first in dignity.

I think you need to consider with us the question before us. Why did God not make man first, since man was to be appointed ruler? Because it was not right to hand the world over to man empty. It had to be in bloom and shining and lacking nothing at all. Brothers, when someone invites a friend to a feast, he first prepares and decorates the house and makes everything ready around the table, and only then brings his guest in to a celebration already prepared. In the same way God first prepared everything and then brought man into his creation: his friend, his own image. And he handed over to him the enjoyment of every good thing.

Besides, brothers, there is another reason why God could not create man before the rest. Adam was not to see how the things that were made came into being, so that he would not become proud. That is why he did not see the variety of the construction. He did not see the earth being set firm, or heaven being raised up, or the sea being given its bounds. He did not see the earth bringing forth cattle and the other beasts. Otherwise he might have become proud, as though the work of creation had been carried out before his eyes. So God makes all created things older than their owner. Because they are older, man would recognize his own lowliness, and because of what was provided for him, he would marvel at the kindness of the Worker of wonders, as I said before.

He made creation and then brought in man. Bodyguards go ahead of a king and the king comes last: last in the order you see, but first in power. In the same way God made creation go before man, and the one made ruler of creation follow after.

But let us come to the very words of the Creator: "Let us make man." Everything else he fashions by a word, as we have heard. God said, "Let there be light," and there was light. He said, "Let there be a firmament," and the word became deed. He said, "Let the earth sprout," and the thing came forth and took on its nature. He said, "Let the waters bring forth birds," and the making ran to meet the command. He said, "Let the earth bring forth four-footed creatures and beasts and creeping things," and all of them came into being in fact. Those other things he brought forth by a word. But when he is about to fashion man, see what he says: "Let us make man in our image and after our likeness." He brings in deliberation as he fashions him, to show that what he is fashioning is something special.

And we must ask, brothers, why in the case of the other created things the account of what happened is followed by proof that the work was done. For example, God said, "Let there be a firmament," and it was so. And God said, "Let there be light," and it was so. And the same holds for the others. With man, however, the account of his making does not fully follow the promise. Pay close attention. God said: "Let us make man in our image and likeness." Following the pattern of what came before, the historian ought to have said here as well, "And it was so." But he did not say this. He reported only half of what was proposed. Does God, then, promise one thing and make another? Far from it! But careful examination opens up for us the meaning of the creation.

He promised to make man in his image and after his likeness. But Scripture did not add "And it was so," leaving much careful contemplation for the eager learner. For all the other creatures he fixed their limits in their nature, but to man he gave free will along with his nature. So he joined "in the image" to man's nature, but entrusted "after the likeness" to his free choice, so that man by his own labors might bring to completion what was promised at his creation. In this way "after the likeness" is fulfilled through a virtuous life and diligence in good works. To show the whole from one part, divine Scripture says: "Be like a father to orphans, and like a husband to their mother, and you will be a son of the Most High."

See how "after the likeness" is completed in keeping the commandments and is rightly left to our free choice. Listen to the evangelist as he lays this down and teaches it. The Lord, wishing to establish the likeness of his own image, says to his disciples: "Be merciful, as your heavenly Father is merciful, and you will be perfect as our Father is perfect." And the apostle says: "Be imitators of God as beloved children, and walk in love, as Christ also loved you." Countless proofs show that the likeness of the image is the perfection of the virtues.

Come, let us again consider the force of what has been said, and examine carefully what this image is and in what "in the image" consists. "God made man in his own image," as Scripture says. In what way, then, is man in the image of God? In the shaping of the body? Far from it! The human body is marked out by limbs and has a shape, but God is simple, without parts, uncompounded and without shape. This common light we see is not marked out by shapes and limbs. It is bright through and through, showing the same evenness and likeness throughout. In the same way God, simple in every respect, without parts and uncompounded, flashes forth through and through as intellectual light.

We must remember that comparisons and examples do not correspond exactly in every respect. The thing being compared is not identical to the comparison. Often the comparison presents what we are looking for through a small and faint image.

But let us come to the matter at hand. If this light that we perceive with our senses is simple and without parts, how much more does the Maker of light go beyond and surpass any simplicity that words can proclaim! So when you hear, "Incline your ear, O Lord, open your eyes and see," do not think that he has ears and eyes like ours. With God, hearing and sight are one and the same. In short, everything said about God is proclaimed as far as our power allows, but cannot be expounded as it deserves [?].

If you find this hearing and seeing hard to grasp, take your understanding from something familiar [?], without relying slavishly on the comparison. The sea is a simple element and appearance. Simple as it looks to us, it does and accomplishes many great things. It roars without a mouth, runs without feet, rises high without wings, holds sailors fast without hands, and seizes many and drowns them without arms. If this element, which looks simple, does so much, how much more does God, who is simple, without parts and without shape, see and hear and act, beyond anything the tongue can express or the reason conceive!

If God is simple, then man cannot be his image in the body. Nor indeed in the soul. Listen to how this is so. The soul often changes. Sometimes its thoughts are self-controlled, sometimes licentious; sometimes just, sometimes unjust; sometimes upright, sometimes perverse. What shifts and changes cannot be the image of the One who says, "I am, and I do not change."

Some people define the mind as something separate from the soul and say that it was made in the image of God, so we must not pass over this argument without examining it. First I state what is held by all who have been brought up in true religion: the mind is considered part of the soul. What the eye is in the body, the mind is in the soul. But some try to distort the doctrine of the soul and bring in the mind as a separate entity, saying that man is made up of three parts: soul, body and mind. Let us convince them that man cannot be in the image, as far as nature goes, even by his mind. Listen to how this is so. Wicked things, frenzy, shameful and unjust things, everything opposed to the virtues, are carried by the mind. Paul bears witness to this when he speaks of the perverse: "men corrupted in mind, worthless in matters of faith." If the human mind can be corrupted, while the mind of the incorruptible God is incorruptible, tell me how it could be his image and likeness.

If, then, man is God's image neither in his soul nor in his mind, "in the image" lies in the commandments. Clearly it also lies in deeds: what man has by nature he receives through the perfection of the virtues. So the Word truly assigned his "in the image and after the likeness" to the virtues. But the first pledge of the image, and the first sign of "in the image," is the honor and dominion over all things that was given to man. God himself explains this. After saying, "Let us make man in our image and after our likeness," he wished to show in what respect he made him in his image, and at once he added: "And let them rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of the sky, the beasts and the cattle and all the earth." That is dominion. [?] is inscribed "in the image,"

and you defile the likeness in our nature [?]. So it is in ruling over all things that man is the image of God: "Let them rule over the fish of the sea and the birds and the beasts and all the earth."

But perhaps the listener will say: "Then where is 'in the image'? Why is not everything subject to man? If we were rulers of all things, even of the beasts, would a lion plot against the image, or a bear attack it, or a leopard or a wild boar or the other, smaller creatures? If we were rulers, a serpent would not bite the one it had received as its ruler, a viper or scorpion would not strike, and no evil beast would plot against the image. Yet we are attacked by all of them." Do not look for the definition of the image after the transgression. Look for its condition before the transgression.

When Adam had not yet transgressed, God brought him all the cattle and all the beasts, and he gave names to them all, like the master of a house naming his servants. The lion was there, fawning on its master. The beasts were there, bowing their heads to their ruler. All the creeping things were there, looking on and honoring the image of God. Even when the king is not present, we honor the king's image. In the same way creation, though it could not see the Invisible One, honored the one made in his image. Water revered him and deferred to him; fire revered him and deferred to him and was abashed. All the beasts recognized him and paid him honor.

But the one made in God's image defaced his own dignity. Forgetting his honor, he lost the original beauty of his creation and made himself like the creatures he ruled. "For man, being in honor, did not understand; he was compared to the senseless cattle and became like them." When he slipped away from the image and was brought down to the likeness of the irrational creatures, it was only natural that those creatures despised him as one of their own. For nothing, brothers, reveres its equal. Rather, it honors one who is superior: it fears him, serves him, bows at his footsteps and blushes at his anger.

So as long as Adam kept the stamp of the divine image, the beasts feared him and kept coming to him, coming as to a master. Today a dog is fierce toward strangers but gentle with its own people. In the same way, as long as Adam ruled while bearing the image, the beasts fawned on him, trembled at his authority and revered his master's face as the image of God. But once he slipped, he was from then on trampled by the irrational creatures and spat upon.

So if he had kept his ancient dignity, the irrational creatures would have remained in their proper subjection. And on this point, so that the one bearing witness may not be thought merely persuasive and his argument contrived, and so that we may not be thought simply to be guessing at the facts because past events are [?] —

if you want to learn that everything would have been subject to man had he remained obedient, take the saints as pledges of the proof. Daniel achieved true piety, and the lions fawned on him, for they saw the stamp restored. Ananias and his companions achieved it, and the fire spread out its back beneath them. The burning flame held back its force, for it saw their piety and honored it. Let us question the fire ourselves, imitating the words of David: "What ails you, O fire, that you fled, and you, O flame, that you turned back?" The fire will answer us accordingly: "I fled from the face of the Lord." For the face of the Lord is the righteous, the image of the truth. For them the fire spread out its back. And to show that it had not changed its nature, but had protected those who bore the stamp of piety, it revered its master inside the furnace, but went outside and devoured the Chaldeans. The flame kept the martyrs unharmed within, but rushed out and swiftly caught the Chaldeans, to show that it had not changed its nature but had honored piety.

And see what is wonderful here. As I have often said to you, fire is a blend of two powers and operations, burning and giving light. As we all know, fire both burns and gives light. So the fire divided its operation. It kept the light for the saints, for "light is always for the saints." But it dealt out the flame to the ungodly, for "coals of fire shall fall upon them; you will cast them down into the fire."

O divine grace, how much it can do! It cuts fire into flame and light. It wrapped the righteous in the light and let the flame loose on the ungodly. And then it truly fulfilled the words of David: "The voice of the One who divides the flame of fire." You see, brother, that creation reveres the royal stamp. How many has the sea drowned? Yet it saw Moses and split apart. The people with him were unworthy of that extraordinary crossing. They did not enter the sea because they had acted righteously, but because of God's love for mankind. David testifies that they entered it unworthy when he says: "And they provoked him as they went up at the Red Sea." Do you see the sea, raging as it was, revering the lawgiver? It spread out its back beneath Moses, because he was the Master's friend. "God spoke to Moses," Scripture says, "as a man speaks to his friend."
See the sea at rest; see the sailors at peace. See the fire at rest. Look, if you like, at the rivers too. And see the proof of the truth shining out from every side.

The river Jordan saw Joshua, who bore the image of the Savior. Seeing his way of life and his name, it split itself and gave passage on dry ground. And these are not the only things shown to be subject to man. Had he remained in the image, the sun too would have been subject to him and the moon would have served him. Experience bears witness to this, and Scripture tells the truth. For Joshua, a man who had restored the stamp through virtue, cried out boldly, "Let the sun stand still!" and a human voice stopped the sun.

In the same way, brothers, snakes and scorpions and serpents now lie in wait for us. They do not hate our nature, but they expose our transgression. Achieve virtue, and you will tread them underfoot. The psalm says to you: "You will tread on the asp and the basilisk, and trample the lion and the serpent." In the same way, brothers, blessed Paul once came to the island of the barbarians. God wished to show the people who did not know him a sign, and he arranged for a viper to come out of the brushwood, fasten onto the saint's right hand and do him no harm. From this very experience they would learn the power of the saints' virtue.

Why, then, did the viper bite Paul, when the lions did not bite Daniel? In Daniel's case it is plain that he had been handed over to destruction. In Paul's case, if the creature had not appeared and bitten him, the worth of the faithful herald would not have been shown. That is why the viper fastened onto his hand while the saint suffered nothing unpleasant. It showed that nothing at all would be able to wrong or harm the image of God. Do you see that, had man remained in the image, all creation would have been subject to him?

But when the Jew hears this, the enemy of the Church, the nursling of the old covenant, he says: "You see how the heralds of the Law trampled on fire! How did Daniel overcome lions? How did the three youths tread on the flame of fire? Why did the martyrs of Christ not come through as the martyrs of the Law did?"

For the enemy, brothers, does not look for the benefit that comes from what is said. He looks for something to seize on against the speaker, something to find or invent against the truth. The Jew, or any other enemy, will at once say: "The righteous men of old far surpass the martyrs of Christ. Wild beasts devoured these, kings put them to the question, the sea drowned them and rivers swallowed them up. But the whole creation stood in awe of the martyrs of the Old Testament."

So, brothers, if they take the fact that the martyrs were handed over to afflictions as a charge of weakness against the Master, let us say to them: "If the martyrs were handed over because of Christ's weakness, then by your own rule you are not being taught [?] because of Christ's weakness. The Maccabees belong to the Old Testament. If it was because of Christ's weakness that they were struck down by those who persecuted the church, and the martyrs were put to death, how is it that he tears down the altars? And how is it that prophets too are put to death and were slaughtered? For Elijah says: 'Lord, they have torn down your altars and killed your prophets, and I alone am left, and they are seeking my life.' If the martyrs were handed over because of Christ's weakness, then those men were too."

But far be it from us to charge the power of Christ with weakness. For our God is mighty, and great is our Lord, and great is his strength. The same order holds for the ancients and for the new. For it is the same God who ordered both the old things and the new. The old things do not belong to the Father and the new to the Son. Both the former and the latter belong to the same Godhead and to the same divine plan. For what does the Father say? "What is yours is mine, and what is mine is yours."

The three young men were rescued from the furnace. The Maccabees were handed over to various tortures. Through those rescued from danger he displayed his own power, and through those who were perfected in martyrdom he proclaimed the steadfastness of true religion. The same can be seen in the new covenant as well. Some martyrs were burned, but other martyrs escaped the flame.

What happened to four saints in two narratives God brought together in a single virgin of the Gospel. Daniel and the three young men divide the wonders between them: he muzzled the lions, and they trampled the fire. But one young virgin of the Gospel bound on her head the crowns of both contests. For Saint Thecla both trampled down wild beasts and quenched the flame of fire.

Many other martyrs too were rescued. Saint Paul fought off countless dangers and escaped them all. Many times he was handed over to death, and the power of Christ rescued its own servant. "If, humanly speaking," he says, "I fought with wild beasts at Ephesus," and again, "I die every day," as far as men are concerned. And again the same man proclaims somewhere: "At my first defense no one stood by me; everyone deserted me. But the Lord stood beside me and gave me strength, and he rescued me from the lion's mouth. And he will rescue me from every kind of evil and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom." To him be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.
